phase1.intro:
Everything up to now has been about handling things going WRONG. Streams are about something different — getting data in and out of files.

Where do you want to start?

topics.buttonText: What exactly is a byte stream?
dialogue: A [[term:byte stream]] moves raw bytes, one at a time or in chunks, with zero interpretation of what those bytes actually mean. [[term:FileInputStream]] reads bytes IN from a file; [[term:FileOutputStream]] writes bytes OUT.
That's genuinely all either one knows how to do — there's no concept of "text" or "encoding" anywhere in a byte stream, just raw numbers.

stickyNote.flavor: 🔢 raw bytes, no idea what they mean
stickyNote.definition: FileInputStream/FileOutputStream move raw bytes in and out of files with zero interpretation — no concept of text or encoding.

topics.buttonText: How do I actually read bytes in a loop?
dialogue: `read()` reads exactly one byte and returns it as an int — [[key:and returns -1 specifically to signal "there's nothing left to read"]], which is why every byte-stream reading loop looks like `while ((byteRead = fis.read()) != -1)`.
`read(byte[] buffer)` is the faster cousin — it fills a whole array in one call instead of looping one byte at a time.

stickyNote.definition: read() returns one byte as an int, or -1 at end of stream. read(byte[]) fills a buffer array in one call for speed.

topics.buttonText: When are byte streams the wrong tool?
dialogue: [[warn:Because byte streams have no idea what encoding means, they're the wrong tool for text]] — use them for genuinely binary data: images, audio, video. [[key:Always close a stream when you're done with it]] — an open handle that never gets released can lock the file.

stickyNote.term: When Not to Use Byte Streams
stickyNote.flavor: 🚫 wrong tool for text, right tool for binary
stickyNote.definition: Byte streams are for genuinely binary data (images, audio) — text needs character streams. Always close a stream when finished.

phase2.errorMessage: (No error shown — but resources leak! The file remains open.)
phase2.explanation:
fis never gets closed. The finally block is there, but it's empty — the comment even says so. That means the file stays open even after the program's logically done with it.

[[warn:this doesn't crash anything, which is exactly what makes it dangerous]] — no error message, no stack trace, nothing that tells you something's wrong. The cost shows up later: the file might stay locked, or if this pattern repeats across a long-running program, you can eventually hit the OS's limit on how many files can be open at once.

[[key:the fix, and honestly the better habit going forward, is try-with-resources]] — instead of a manual finally block with a null check, try (FileInputStream fis = new FileInputStream("data.bin")) { ... } closes fis automatically the instant the block ends, no matter how it ends.
phase2.openingDialogue: Watch what happens when a stream never gets closed~

phase3.openingDialogue: Let's move some raw bytes ourselves~

mcq.question:
What does read() return when a byte stream reaches the end of a file?

A) 0
B) null
C) -1
D) It throws an exception

phase4.selfChallenge:
Write a program that:
1. Creates an array of bytes: {10, 20, 30, 40, 50}
2. Writes these bytes to a file called "numbers.bin" using FileOutputStream
3. Reads the bytes back using FileInputStream
4. Prints each byte with its decimal value

Use try-with-resources for both operations.

phase5.trivia: [[fun:Fun fact]]: byte streams are the oldest I/O classes in Java, dating back to Java 1.0 in 1996 — character streams (Reader/Writer) weren't added until 1.1, specifically because the original design underestimated how much text-encoding handling real programs would need.
phase5.openingDialogue: One more thought before you go~
